opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to where the bottleneck is. Hardware has improved enormously over the past few years. You can buy a fairly capable humanoid or a robot arm now, and the cost keeps falling. But when you put these machines in a real environment, like a kitchen, a warehouse, or someone's living room, they still can't do much. The body is often good enough. What's missing is the intelligence: understanding the world, reasoning about space and physics, and planning over long horizons.

My background is in computer vision and representation learning, so for me the most natural question is how a system perceives and models the world. I've always believed that visual intelligence, or spatial intelligence more broadly, is the foundation for physical intelligence. Language models gave us something remarkable, but language is a compressed, human-curated view of reality. A robot has to deal with the raw world: continuous, messy, three-dimensional, constantly changing. That's a vision and world-modeling problem first.

There's also a practical reason. Hardware is capital-intensive and slow to iterate, and it requires a very different kind of team and supply chain. If you tie yourself to one body too early, you risk overfitting your whole research agenda to that platform. If you work on the brain, ideally in a way that can generalize across embodiments, you're betting on something more durable. Bodies will keep changing. A good world model and a good perception system should transfer.

That doesn't mean hardware isn't important. We'll obviously need close collaboration with people building robots, and real-world data from real bodies matters a lot. But in terms of where my comparative advantage lies, and where I think the deepest unsolved scientific questions are, it's the brain. That's where I want to spend my time.

r001.rationale: The response says robot hardware is often capable enough while intelligence remains the bottleneck, describes deep unsolved questions in perception and world modeling, and says that is why the speaker wants to focus on the brain.

r002.rationale: It mentions close collaboration with robot builders and the importance of real-world data, but does not state that partnerships provide closed-loop robot validation.

r003.rationale: It says hardware is capital-intensive and slow to iterate, but does not identify acquiring many robots as a requirement for scaling robotics hardware.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to where I believe the real bottleneck is, and where I can actually make a difference.

If you look at robotics today, the hardware has gotten remarkably good. We have humanoids that can walk, hands with impressive dexterity, actuators and sensors that are cheaper and more capable every year. Hardware is improving on a fairly predictable engineering curve, and there are a lot of excellent teams working on it. But if you put the most sophisticated robot body in a kitchen and ask it to do something it hasn't seen before, it mostly just stands there. The body isn't the problem. The problem is that the robot doesn't understand the world it's in.

That's a representation learning problem, and that's really my background. My whole career has been about how machines perceive and build internal models of the visual world, from ConvNeXt to the work on world models and spatial understanding. Robotics is in some sense the ultimate test of whether those representations actually mean anything. In a benchmark, a model can get away with shortcuts. A robot can't. It has to understand depth, physics, object permanence, cause and effect, what happens when I push this thing. So for me, the robot brain isn't a departure from vision research, it's the natural destination of it.

There's also a practical reason. Hardware is capital intensive and iteration is slow. You build one robot, you break it, you wait weeks for parts. If you tie your intelligence research to a specific hardware platform too early, you end up over-fitting to that body and that lab setup. I'd rather build the general capability, the ability to perceive and reason about space and action, in a way that can transfer across many embodiments, and let the hardware ecosystem mature in parallel. I think the right analogy is language models: nobody built a new kind of computer to make them work. The intelligence was the hard part, and once it existed, the hardware integration followed.

And honestly, as an academic, I have to pick my battles. I can't compete with a well-funded company on manufacturing. But on the question of how a system learns to understand the physical world from data, from video, from interaction, I think a university lab can still make foundational contributions. So that's where I want to put my effort. The body will be there when the brain is ready.

r001.rationale: The response says robots still fail because they do not understand the world, describes that understanding as a hard representation-learning problem, and uses this to justify building general robot intelligence before tying research to hardware.

r002.rationale: It says robotics is a test of whether representations work, but does not state that partnerships provide the closed-loop validation needed for robot-brain research.

r003.rationale: It describes hardware as capital intensive and iteration as slow, but does not identify acquiring many robots as a requirement for scaling hardware work.

astra-6.text:
我觉得现阶段最核心的问题还是智能。机器人硬件当然很重要，但如果它不能理解环境、理解人的意图，也不能在新的场景里完成任务，那即使身体做得很好，它能发挥的作用也比较有限。

所以我更想先把“大脑”这件事做好：怎么把感知、推理和行动连接起来，让机器人不只是重复一个预先设定的动作，而是能够学习、适应变化。这个问题本身已经足够难了。如果太早同时投入硬件，机械、控制、制造这些事情都会占用很多精力，研究的重心也容易被某一种具体的机器人形态绑定。

当然，大脑不可能完全脱离身体来研究，我们还是需要在真实的硬件上验证。但我希望先聚焦在智能这一层，和做硬件的人合作，把最关键的问题往前推。

r001.rationale: The response says robot intelligence remains the core unresolved challenge, that building the brain is already difficult, and that hardware work would consume focus, supporting prioritizing intelligence research first.

r002.rationale: It says real hardware is needed for validation and mentions collaborating with hardware makers, but does not clearly state that those partnerships provide closed-loop robot validation.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that scaling robotics hardware requires acquiring many robots.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is where we can contribute the most. Building a robot involves a lot of difficult hardware and engineering work, and if we take all of that on early, it can pull our attention away from the intelligence problem.

By focusing on the brain, we can ask: How does a robot understand what it sees, learn from experience, and turn that understanding into useful actions? Of course, you can’t completely separate that from the body. You need real hardware to test your ideas, because the physical world will expose assumptions that look fine in simulation. But using hardware and developing hardware are different commitments. I’d rather start with existing platforms, learn what the intelligence actually requires, and let that inform any deeper hardware involvement later.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes brain research to focus on the intelligence problem, describing how robots understand, learn, and act before taking on deeper hardware work.

r002.rationale: It says real hardware is needed for testing and suggests using existing platforms, but does not mention partnerships or closed-loop validation.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that doing hardware well requires acquiring many robots.
